# Effective Prompting

## Good Enough Prompting {.band-bottom}

::: {.lead}
Most of the prompt engineering advice from a few years ago is now either useless
or actively harmful.
:::

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Say what you want, not how to do it]{.card-title}

"I want to compare revenue across countries --- how should we show it?"

beats

"Make a bar chart, sorted descending, gridlines off, 12pt labels."
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[If it does not work, try again]{.card-title}

Rephrasing is cheap. Treat it as an infinitely patient colleague with a poor memory.
:::
:::

## Plan Before You Act {.compare}

Say: plan how to do this before you start.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Why it works --- knowledge]{.eyebrow}

Planning pulls the relevant considerations into the conversation. It then
answers in light of what it just retrieved.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Why it works --- subtasks]{.eyebrow}

It breaks the work into steps you can check one at a time. Failures stay small
and local instead of surfacing at the very end.
:::
::::

## Confirm It Understood

::: {.lead}
Ambiguity does not produce a question. It produces a confident answer to a
question you did not ask.
:::

[Tell GLM, before it starts]{.eyebrow}

> Tell me what you are about to do and what you are assuming.

::: {.note}
Correct it in one sentence, then say go ahead. This is the cheapest habit in the
course and it will save you the most time.
:::

## It Is a Prediction Machine, Not a Colleague {.compare}

Suppose it told you last week that method A beats method B. Today you ask it to
do the task.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[What it will do]{.eyebrow}

If "A beats B" is not in this conversation, and B appeared more often in its
training data, it will probably use B.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Why]{.eyebrow}

Knowledge in the weights is not knowledge in use. Something has to pull it into
the conversation before it can act on it.
:::
::::

## Tunnel Vision {.band-bottom}

::: {.lead}
Prediction also means momentum. Once it has started down a path, continuing that
path is the likeliest next step.
:::

You will watch it hit a roadblock, find a way around, hit another, find another
way around --- tenaciously, exhaustively. What it rarely does is go back and ask
whether a different path was better all along.

::: {.note .note-plum}
Restate the goal, not the obstacle. That gives it permission to abandon the path
instead of defending it.
:::

## What Not to Do {.plain-title}

| Skip | Why |
|---|---|
| "Think step by step" | Reasoning models already do, in hidden tokens |
| "Take a deep breath" | Measurably useless now |
| "CRITICAL! NEVER EVER ..." | Overtriggers, and gets worse results |
| Stacked personas | "You are an expert X" can help tone; three of them does not |

::: {.note}
Direct task framing wins. Say what you want, say what done looks like, say what to avoid.
:::

# AI and Coding

## Anatomy of a Chatbot {.band-bottom}

::: {.chatbot-architecture}
::: {.arch-box .arch-plum .arch-left}
You
:::
::: {.arch-arrow .arch-a}
&#8596;
:::
::: {.arch-box .arch-blue .arch-mid}
Chatbot
:::
::: {.arch-arrow .arch-b}
&#8596;
:::
::: {.arch-box .arch-plum .arch-right}
The model
:::
:::

The model reads text and writes text. That is the entire capability.

::: {.note .note-plum}
It cannot open a file, run a calculation, look up today's price, or check
whether what it just told you is true.
:::

## An Agent Is a Chatbot with Tools {.plain-title}

::: {.agent-architecture}
::: {.arch-box .arch-tool .arch-up-box}
Code execution
:::
::: {.arch-arrow .arch-arrow-v .arch-up-arrow}
&#8597;
:::
::: {.arch-box .arch-plum .arch-left}
You
:::
::: {.arch-arrow .arch-a}
&#8596;
:::
::: {.arch-box .arch-blue .arch-mid}
Agent
:::
::: {.arch-arrow .arch-b}
&#8596;
:::
::: {.arch-box .arch-plum .arch-right}
The model
:::
::: {.arch-arrow .arch-arrow-v .arch-dn-arrow}
&#8597;
:::
::: {.arch-box .arch-tool .arch-dn-box}
Other tools
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
[The model never runs any of it]{.accent} --- it only emits requests.
:::

## The Loop, Step by Step {.band-bottom}

::: {.steps}
1. The agent sends the prompt, the history, and a list of tools it has
2. The model answers: use tool X, with these arguments
3. The agent runs tool X and reports the result back, with instructions for reading it
4. The model decides what to do next --- another tool, or an answer for you
:::

::: {.note}
The model emits requests; the agent executes them. Those step-3 instructions
are the tool harness, and some are far better than others.
:::




## Writing and Running Code {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
Almost everything useful the model does, it does by writing code and running it, including terminal commands.
:::

> On our AI lab, GLM will write code, save it to a file (a tool use), then run it with a terminal command (another tool use), read the output (another tool use), and revise and repeat as necessary.

All of this is orchestrated by the Claude Code "harness."

# Git and GitHub 


## Git Is a Version Control System {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
A commit is a snapshot of the whole folder, dated and labelled. Nothing is ever
overwritten --- it is added to.
:::

::: {.note}
Every commit is a point you can go back to, and Git can tell you what changed
between any two of them, in which file, and on which line.
:::

Git is not an AI tool. It is twenty years older than any of this. GLM simply
knows how to drive it.


## Git vs GitHub {.compare}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Git]{.eyebrow}

On your machine. The history lives in the folder itself --- no network, no
account, yours alone.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[GitHub]{.eyebrow}

A hosted copy of that same history for backup and sharing.
:::
::::

## Create an Account and Log In from the Lab {.plain-title}


::: {.steps}
1. Create a free account at `github.com`, and note your username
2. Open the Terminal tab, not the GLM pane --- this step waits for you to type
3. Run `gh auth login` and answer: GitHub.com, HTTPS, yes to authenticating Git, browser
4. It prints a code --- open the link on your laptop and paste it there
:::



## One Person in Each Group Does This

[Tell GLM --- one person in the group, once]{.eyebrow}

- Make a folder in my workspace called [whatever you want to call it] and make it a git repository. 

- Add a .gitignore for csv, parquet, and .env files. 

- Commit, then create a private GitHub repo of the same name and push to it.

## Then Add Your Groupmates

[On github.com, in the new repository]{.eyebrow}

::: {.steps}
1. Settings, then Collaborators, then Add people
2. Search each groupmate by their GitHub username
3. They get an email invitation, and have to accept it
:::


## Everyone Else Joins {.band-bottom}

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Clone the GitHub repo [username]/[repo name] into my workspace.  

> username should be the username of the group member who created it. repo name is the name they used for the folder


## Later: Push and Pull

[Tell GLM, at the start of every session]{.eyebrow}

> Pull the latest from GitHub before we start.

[Then, at the end of the session]{.eyebrow}

> Commit what we did and push it.


## When Git Pushes Back {.plain-title}

| What you see | What to say |
|---|---|
| `rejected --- non-fast-forward` | Someone pushed while you were working. "Pull their work, merge it, then push." |
| `CONFLICT: automatic merge failed` | You both edited the same lines. "Show me both versions and wait for me to choose." |

::: {.note .note-plum}
Refuse these if asked: `git push --force` and `git reset --hard`
:::
